blocks.title: Addition polymerisation
blocks.text: In addition polymerisation, monomers add to each other one by one, forming long chains. All the atoms of the monomers become part of the polymer; nothing is lost and no side product such as water forms.

The monomers must have a C=C (or C triple bond C) bond, which opens up to let the monomers link together. The process is often a chain reaction started by a very reactive molecule, an initiator, which forms free radicals. For example, many ethene molecules join end to end: n CH2=CH2 -> [-CH2-CH2-]n (initiator, heat, pressure), where n is very large, up to about 10 000.

blocks.alt: Top: n CH2=CH2 + initiator, with heat/pressure over the arrow, gives [-CH2-CH2-]n; labels ethene and poly(ethene). Below: n displayed ethene, H2C=CH2 with an H on each corner, gives the bracketed displayed repeat unit -C(H)(H)-C(H)(H)- with subscript n. 'Where n is very large, e.g. up to 10 000'.
blocks.caption: Formation of poly(ethene) from ethene (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 146).

blocks.text: Poly(ethene) is mainly of two types. Low density poly(ethene) (LDPE) is used where a very light, soft material is needed, such as shopping bags and light plastic bottles. High density poly(ethene) (HDPE) is made from ethene at low pressure and temperature with a Ziegler-Natta catalyst and is used for plastic containers, thick shopping bags and toys. LDPE chains are more branched, so they cannot pack tightly, giving a less solid, more elastic material; HDPE chains are linear and pack closely, giving a tough, dense structure.

blocks.title: Did you know?
blocks.text: Ziegler-Natta catalysts are a Nobel Prize-winning invention that changed plastic production. Karl Ziegler discovered them in 1953; they made the low-pressure polymerisation of ethene into linear HDPE possible, and Giulio Natta extended them to stereoregular polymers such as crystalline polypropene.
PVC is made from chloroethene by addition polymerisation: n CH2=CHCl -> [-CH2-CHCl-]n.

blocks.alt: Top: n CH2=CHCl + initiator gives [-CH2-CHCl-]n; labels chloroethene and poly(chloroethene) or PVC. Below: three displayed chloroethene molecules (Cl and H on one carbon, two H on the other) give a displayed chain of six carbons with Cl on every second carbon and H on all the others.
blocks.caption: Formation of PVC from chloroethene, condensed and detailed (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 147).

blocks.text: Its properties can be changed a lot by adding plasticisers, chemicals that make materials softer, more flexible and easier to work with, by reducing the strong forces between polymer chains. Rigid PVC (without plasticisers) is hard and stiff, chemically inert to most acids, bases and oils, a good electrical insulator, naturally resistant to burning (self-extinguishing) because of its chlorine atoms, and long-lasting. Plasticised PVC is flexible and soft and can be bent and shaped easily, while keeping good chemical and electrical properties.

items: Pipes and fittings for water supply, drainage and sewage, because it resists corrosion and lasts.
Window frames, door profiles and vinyl floor tiles and sheets.
Electrical insulation for wires and cables.
Cling films, bottles (e.g. for cooking oil) and blister packs.
Raincoats, artificial leather and inflatable products such as swimming pools.
